title: Light Energy
summary: Light is the form of energy that makes things visible. Objects that give out their own light (sun, candle, firefly) are luminous; others (moon, a steel plate) are seen by the light they reflect. Reflection is the bouncing back of light from a surface; a smooth, shiny surface that reflects most light is a mirror. Laws of reflection: (1) the incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal at the point of incidence lie in the same plane; (2) the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection (∠i = ∠r). Speed, frequency and wavelength do not change on reflection. A smooth surface gives regular reflection; a rough surface scatters light in all directions (diffused reflection), though each ray still obeys the laws.

A real image is formed where reflected (or refracted) rays actually meet; it can be taken on a screen. A virtual image is formed where rays only appear to meet; it cannot be taken on a screen. A plane mirror forms a virtual, erect image of the same size, as far behind the mirror as the object is in front, and laterally inverted (left appears right). If the object moves towards the mirror at v, the image moves towards the object at 2v. A mirror half your height is enough to see your full image.

A spherical mirror is part of a hollow sphere: in a concave mirror the reflecting surface curves inward; in a convex mirror it bulges outward. Terms: pole (P) — centre of the mirror; centre of curvature (C); radius of curvature (R) = PC; principal axis — line through P and C; principal focus (F) — where rays parallel to the axis meet after reflection (concave) or appear to come from (convex); focal length f = PF, with R = 2f. Rays used in diagrams: a ray parallel to the axis passes through (or appears to come from) F; a ray through F becomes parallel; a ray through C returns along its path; a ray to the pole reflects at an equal angle.

Concave mirror: object at infinity — image at F, real, inverted, highly diminished; beyond C — between F and C, real, inverted, diminished; at C — at C, real, inverted, same size; between C and F — beyond C, real, inverted, enlarged; at F — at infinity, highly enlarged; between F and P — behind the mirror, virtual, erect, enlarged. Convex mirror: for any position the image is behind the mirror between P and F, virtual, erect and diminished.

Uses: plane mirrors in looking glasses, periscopes and kaleidoscopes; concave mirrors in torches, searchlights and vehicle headlights, solar cookers, shaving and dentists' mirrors, reflecting telescopes; convex mirrors as rear-view mirrors in vehicles and at dangerous corners, because they always give an erect, smaller image of a wide field of view.

Sign convention: all distances are measured from the pole; distances in the direction of incident light are positive and opposite to it negative; heights above the axis are positive. Mirror formula: 1/f = 1/v + 1/u. Magnification m = height of image / height of object (= −v/u for a mirror).

Refraction is the bending of light when it passes obliquely from one medium to another, because its speed changes. Going from a rarer to a denser medium (air to glass) light slows down and bends towards the normal; from denser to rarer it speeds up and bends away from the normal. A ray falling along the normal goes straight. A coin in water looks raised for this reason. Frequency (and colour) do not change; speed and wavelength do. Laws: (1) the incident ray, refracted ray and normal lie in one plane; (2) Snell's law — sin i / sin r is a constant, the refractive index n. Also n = speed of light in vacuum / speed of light in the medium; light is slowest in the medium with the largest n. A diamond sparkles because of its very high refractive index.

A lens is a transparent medium bounded by two surfaces, at least one curved. A convex (converging) lens is thicker in the middle and brings parallel rays to a focus; a concave (diverging) lens is thinner in the middle and spreads them out as if from a focus. Rays used: a ray parallel to the axis passes through (or appears to come from) the focus; a ray through the optical centre goes straight.

Convex lens: object at infinity — image at F, real, inverted, highly diminished; beyond 2F — between F and 2F, real, inverted, diminished; at 2F — at 2F, real, inverted, same size; between F and 2F — beyond 2F, real, inverted, enlarged; at F — at infinity; between F and the optical centre — on the same side, virtual, erect, enlarged (a magnifying glass). Concave lens: always a virtual, erect, diminished image between F and the lens.

Lens formula: 1/f = 1/v − 1/u (f positive for a convex lens, negative for a concave lens). Magnification m = h′/h = v/u. Power of a lens P = 1/f (f in metres); its unit is the dioptre (D). A convex lens has positive power, a concave lens negative. Example: an object 20 cm from a convex lens of focal length 15 cm gives an image 60 cm on the other side, real, inverted and three times as large. A lens of focal length 10 cm gives an image of the same size when the object is at 2F, i.e. 20 cm away.

When white light passes through a glass prism it splits into seven colours — violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange, red (VIBGYOR); this is dispersion. It happens because the refractive index of glass is different for different colours, so they bend by different amounts: violet bends the most and red the least. The band of colours is a spectrum. A rainbow is formed by dispersion of sunlight by raindrops. Visible light has wavelengths about 400–700 nm; longer than red is infrared and shorter than violet is ultraviolet.

The eye lens forms a real, inverted, diminished image on the retina; the ciliary muscles change its focal length so that both near and far objects are seen clearly — the power of accommodation. A normal eye sees from infinity (far point) to 25 cm (near point, the least distance of distinct vision). The visual angle is the angle an object makes at the eye; distant objects look small because their visual angle is small. The eye is relaxed when looking at far objects.

Myopia (short-sightedness): distant objects are not clear because the image forms in front of the retina; corrected with a concave (diverging) lens of negative power. Hypermetropia (long-sightedness): near objects are not clear because the image forms behind the retina; corrected with a convex (converging) lens of positive power. Presbyopia: in old age the muscles weaken and both near and far vision suffer; corrected with bifocal lenses. Astigmatism: the eye lens is not perfectly spherical, so lines in different directions are not seen clearly together; corrected with cylindrical lenses. A person using a +2 D lens is long-sighted; one using a −2 D lens is short-sighted.

Between F and the optical centre

objective: Write True (T) or False (F): (1) The image formed by a plane mirror is real and inverted. (2) The image formed by a plane mirror is behind the mirror at a distance equal to the distance of the object from the mirror.
(1) False — it is virtual and erect. (2) True
Fill in the blanks: In a concave lens, the image distance is always ________ and the image formed is ________.
negative (on the same side as the object); virtual, erect and diminished

Read the passage and answer: 'Magnification is the ratio of the height of the image to the height of the object. It can also be expressed through the image distance and object distance. A student uses a lens to form an image with magnification +1.5.' (1) Which describes the image? (A) Real and inverted (B) Virtual and smaller (C) Virtual and larger (D) Real and upright. (2) What does a negative magnification indicate?
(1) (C) Virtual and larger (positive m means erect, i.e. virtual; 1.5 means larger). (2) A negative magnification means the image is real and inverted.
Fill in the blanks: When light goes from a rarer to a denser medium it bends ________ the normal, and the ratio sin i / sin r is called the ________ of the medium.
Match: (1) Concave mirror (2) Convex mirror — (a) rear-view mirror (b) periscope (c) headlight reflector (d) magnifying glass
(1) Concave mirror – (c) headlight reflector; (2) Convex mirror – (a) rear-view mirror
Write True (T) or False (F): (1) Hypermetropia is corrected with a convex lens. (2) The image formed by the eye lens on the retina is erect.
(1) True (2) False — it is real and inverted.

case.passage: Some people cannot see distant objects clearly, while others struggle to see nearby objects. These conditions arise from changes in the shape of the eye or problems with the eye lens, so that the image is not formed on the retina. Concave or convex lenses of suitable power bring the focus back onto the retina and form clear images. A student complains that he cannot see the blackboard clearly but can read his book easily.

The lens that will correct his vision is a —

The ability of the eye to see both near and far objects clearly by changing the focal length of its lens is called —

vsa: Write two characteristics of an image formed by a plane mirror.
(1) It is virtual and erect, and of the same size as the object. (2) It is as far behind the mirror as the object is in front, and laterally inverted.

or: Draw ray diagrams of a myopic eye and its correction.

Myopic eye: parallel rays from a distant object meet in front of the retina. Corrected eye: a concave lens placed before the eye spreads the rays slightly so that the eye lens now brings them to a focus on the retina.

vsa: In a lens of focal length 10 cm the sizes of the image and the object are the same. Name the type of lens and give the distance of the object from the lens.
It is a convex lens, since only a convex lens gives an image of the same size (real and inverted). The object is at 2F, i.e. 2 × 10 = 20 cm from the lens.

or: Define (i) visual angle and (ii) power of accommodation.

(i) Visual angle is the angle an object makes at the eye; the larger it is, the bigger the object looks. (ii) Power of accommodation is the ability of the eye lens to change its focal length so as to see objects from infinity down to 25 cm clearly.

vsa: Draw a ray diagram to show the formation of an enlarged, erect image of a tiny object by a concave mirror.

Place the object between the pole P and the focus F. A ray parallel to the axis reflects through F; a ray from the object towards the mirror along the line from C reflects back on itself. The reflected rays diverge; extended behind the mirror they meet, giving a virtual, erect, enlarged image behind the mirror.
Draw a ray diagram to show image formation by a convex mirror when the object is between its centre of curvature and principal focus.

A ray parallel to the axis reflects as if coming from F behind the mirror; a ray directed towards C reflects back along itself. Extended behind the mirror, the reflected rays meet between P and F: the image is virtual, erect and diminished.
Draw a ray diagram to show the formation of a small, erect image of vehicles behind a car in its rear-view mirror.

The rear-view mirror is convex. Rays from a vehicle behind strike the mirror; a ray parallel to the axis reflects as if from F, and a ray towards C reflects back on itself. Their backward extensions meet behind the mirror between P and F, giving a virtual, erect, small image — so a wide view of the road behind is seen.
Draw ray diagrams showing image formation by a convex lens when the object is placed (a) beyond 2F (b) between the optical centre and the focus.

(a) Beyond 2F: a ray parallel to the axis passes through F on the other side; a ray through the optical centre goes straight; they meet between F and 2F — real, inverted, diminished image. (b) Between O and F: the refracted rays diverge; extended back they meet on the same side as the object — virtual, erect, enlarged image (magnifying glass).

vsa.note: October 2022 asked only for case (b): the convex lens as a magnifier.

sa: An object is placed at 10 cm from a convex mirror of radius of curvature 30 cm. Find the position and nature of the image.
f = R/2 = +15 cm (convex), u = −10 cm. 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = 1/15 + 1/10 = 5/30, so v = +6 cm. The image is 6 cm behind the mirror; it is virtual, erect and diminished (m = −v/u = 0.6).

sa.note: October 2019 asked the same for an object 10 cm from a convex mirror of focal length 20 cm: 1/v = 1/20 + 1/10 = 3/20, v ≈ +6.7 cm behind the mirror, virtual, erect, diminished.

sa: An object is placed 20 cm from a convex lens of focal length 15 cm, perpendicular to its principal axis. Find the nature and position of the image.
f = +15 cm, u = −20 cm. 1/v = 1/f + 1/u = 1/15 − 1/20 = 1/60, so v = +60 cm. The image is 60 cm on the other side of the lens; it is real, inverted and magnified (m = v/u = −3, three times as large).
Draw a labelled ray diagram for a concave mirror when the object is between C and F. Give the location, nature, orientation and size of the image.
A ray parallel to the axis reflects through F; a ray through F reflects parallel to the axis; they meet beyond C. (a) Location: beyond C. (b) Real. (c) Inverted. (d) Enlarged.
Explain the dispersion of white light by a glass prism with a labelled ray diagram. Name a natural phenomenon based on dispersion.

When a narrow beam of white light passes through a prism it splits into seven colours (VIBGYOR) because the refractive index of glass is different for each colour; violet bends the most and red the least. Diagram: white light enters one face, bends towards the base and emerges as a fan of colours with red at the top and violet at the bottom on a screen. Natural example: the rainbow, formed by dispersion of sunlight in raindrops.
What is refraction of light? State the laws of refraction.

Refraction is the bending of light when it passes obliquely from one transparent medium to another, because its speed changes. Laws: (1) the incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal at the point of incidence lie in the same plane; (2) the ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction is constant for a given pair of media (Snell's law), equal to the refractive index.
Reema claims to have obtained an image twice the size of the object with a concave lens. Is she correct? A lens forms an erect, magnified and virtual image — name the lens.

No. A concave lens always forms a virtual, erect and diminished image, never a magnified one. The lens forming an erect, magnified, virtual image is a convex lens with the object between its focus and optical centre.
la: (a) Define dispersion of white light through a glass prism and draw a diagram. (b) Which colour bends the least and which the most? (c) Why does a prism show dispersion of white light? (d) Write the nature of the image formed by a concave lens.

(a) The splitting of white light into its seven constituent colours on passing through a prism is dispersion. Diagram: white light entering a triangular prism, bending towards the base and emerging as a spread spectrum — red at the top, violet at the bottom. (b) Red bends (deviates) the least; violet the most. (c) The refractive index of glass is different for different colours (wavelengths), so each colour is bent through a different angle and they separate. A rainbow is a natural example. (d) A concave lens always forms a virtual, erect and diminished image on the same side as the object, between its focus and the lens.

or: Draw diagrams of a double convex, plano-convex, double concave and convexo-concave lens, and of a myopic eye, a hypermetropic eye and a relaxed normal eye.

Lenses: double convex — both faces bulge out; plano-convex — one flat, one bulging; double concave — both faces curve in; convexo-concave — one face bulges, the other curves in (a meniscus). Eyes: myopic — parallel rays focus in front of the retina; hypermetropic — rays from a near object focus behind the retina; relaxed normal eye — parallel rays from a distant object focus exactly on the retina.

la: Identify the device used in each case when the image formed is enlarged, virtual and erect: (a) object between the device and its focus, image behind it; (b) object between the device and its focus, image on the same side as the object. Draw ray diagrams for each.

(a) A concave mirror, with the object between its pole and focus: the reflected rays diverge and appear to come from a point behind the mirror, giving a virtual, erect, enlarged image. (b) A convex lens (magnifying glass), with the object between its optical centre and focus: the refracted rays diverge and appear to come from a point on the object's side, giving a virtual, erect, enlarged image.
Draw ray diagrams showing image formation by (a) a concave mirror and (b) a convex mirror when the object is beyond the centre of curvature. Give the nature of the image in each case.

(a) Concave mirror: a ray parallel to the axis reflects through F; a ray through C reflects back on itself; they meet between F and C — the image is real, inverted and diminished. (b) Convex mirror: a ray parallel to the axis reflects as if from F behind the mirror; a ray towards C reflects back; the extensions meet behind the mirror between P and F — the image is virtual, erect and diminished.

la.note: April 2017 also asked for an object between O and F of a concave lens (virtual, erect, diminished), at 2F of a convex lens (real, inverted, same size at 2F) and at C of a concave mirror (real, inverted, same size at C).
